nameStory: Gloeochaete wittrockiana doesn't have a widely-used common name, which isn't surprising since it's a microscopic freshwater alga that most people never encounter. The scientific name honors Veit Brecher Wittrock, a Swedish botanist who studied algae in the late 1800s. The genus name 'Gloeochaete' comes from Greek words meaning 'sticky bristles,' referring to the hair-like structures that extend from this tiny organism.
description: This is not actually a plant you can spot during a nature walk - Gloeochaete wittrockiana is a microscopic single-celled alga that lives in freshwater. It's incredibly tiny, only visible under a microscope, where it appears as small round cells with distinctive bristle-like projections called setae. Each cell is typically less than 20 micrometers across - that's smaller than the width of a human hair! Despite its size, it's considered quite important scientifically as it represents an ancient lineage of algae.

idTips.label: Microscopic size
idTips.description: Completely invisible to the naked eye - you'll need a microscope to see individual cells, which appear as tiny spheres

idTips.label: Bristle-like setae
idTips.description: Under magnification, long hair-like projections extend from the cell surface, giving it a spiky appearance like a tiny sea urchin

idTips.label: Spherical cells
idTips.description: Individual cells are roughly round or oval-shaped when viewed under the microscope

idTips.label: Freshwater habitat
idTips.description: Found floating in pond water, lake samples, or slow-moving streams - never in salt water

habitat: Lives in freshwater environments including ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams throughout New England. You'd need to collect water samples and examine them under a microscope to find this species. It's typically found in the plankton - the community of tiny organisms that float freely in the water column.

funFact: This tiny alga is considered a 'living fossil' that may represent what some of the earliest plant ancestors looked like over a billion years ago - it's like finding a microscopic time capsule floating in your local pond!
confusionNotes: Under the microscope, it could be confused with other small algae, but the distinctive long bristles (setae) extending from spherical cells make it unique. The bristles are much longer and more prominent than the short projections found on most other microscopic algae.
contextualKnowledge: While called an alga, Gloeochaete is actually quite different from typical green algae and represents a very ancient evolutionary branch. It's of particular interest to scientists studying how complex plant cells evolved, making this humble pond-dweller more scientifically important than its tiny size might suggest.
compareHints: Since it's the only Gloeochaete species commonly found in New England waters, compare it with other microscopic freshwater algae. Unlike typical green algae which have smooth cell walls, Gloeochaete has those characteristic long bristles. Unlike blue-green algae (cyanobacteria), it has a true cell nucleus and more complex internal structure.
